title: Ohm's Law: Voltage, Current, and Resistance
learning_objectives: Define voltage, current, and resistance and their units
State Ohm's Law and rearrange it to solve for any one quantity
Calculate current, voltage, or resistance given the other two
Explain what happens to current when voltage or resistance changes
Recognize safe and unsafe current values for small components
introduction: Every circuit you build is governed by one simple relationship: Ohm's Law. It connects the three quantities you will measure most often — voltage, current, and resistance — and lets you predict how a circuit will behave before you power it on.
real_world_application: When you power an LED from a 5 V supply, you need a resistor to limit the current. Ohm's Law tells you exactly which resistor value keeps the LED safe. Without it, you would guess and risk burning the component.

core_concepts.definition: The electrical pressure that pushes charge through a circuit. Measured in volts (V).
The rate at which charge flows. Measured in amperes (A), often milliamps (mA).
The opposition to current flow. Measured in ohms (O).
V = I × R. Voltage equals current multiplied by resistance.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Identify the three quantities: voltage (V), current (I), and resistance (R).
2. Write Ohm's Law: V = I × R.
3. To find current: I = V / R.
4. To find resistance: R = V / I.
6. Check the result against safe operating ranges for your components.

important_formulas.name: Ohm's Law
important_formulas.variables: V = volts, I = amperes, R = ohms

important_formulas.name: Current
important_formulas.variables: I = amperes, V = volts, R = ohms

important_formulas.name: Resistance
important_formulas.variables: R = ohms, V = volts, I = amperes

wiring_instructions: No physical wiring required for this lesson. The interactive experiment uses a simulated circuit.
diagram_specification: A simple circuit diagram showing a voltage source connected across a resistor, with labels for V, I, and R.

interactive_experiment.description: Adjust voltage and resistance sliders to see the calculated current update in real time.
interactive_experiment.expected_behavior: Increasing voltage increases current. Increasing resistance decreases current.

expected_observations: Current increases when voltage increases (at fixed resistance).
Current decreases when resistance increases (at fixed voltage).
Doubling voltage doubles current (at fixed resistance).
Doubling resistance halves current (at fixed voltage).
common_mistakes: Confusing voltage and current — voltage is the push, current is the flow.
Forgetting that current depends on both voltage AND resistance.
Using ohms when the value is in kiloohms without converting.
Assuming a resistor alone sets current without considering the supply voltage.
troubleshooting_steps: If current seems too high: check that resistance is not too low.
If current seems too low: check that voltage is applied and resistance is not too high.
Verify units: V in volts, R in ohms, I in amperes (not milliamps).
safety_notes: In real circuits, always check component current ratings before applying power.
Small LEDs typically need 10-20 mA. Exceeding this can damage the LED.
Resistors have power ratings (e.g., 1/4 W). Exceeding this can cause overheating.

knowledge_check.question: A 9 V battery is applied across a 330 O resistor. Approximately how much current flows?
If you double the resistance while keeping voltage the same, what happens to current?
knowledge_check.explanation: From I = V / R, if R doubles and V is constant, I becomes V / (2R) = I/2.

mini_challenge: Using Ohm's Law, work out the resistor needed to limit an LED to 20 mA from a 5 V supply (assume a 2 V LED drop). Hint: the resistor sees 3 V.
extension_activity: Research how temperature affects resistance in thermistors and how this is used in temperature sensors.
assumptions: Ideal components with no temperature dependence.
intended_learning_outcome: Learner can calculate voltage, current, or resistance using Ohm's Law and explain the inverse relationship between current and resistance.
